summary: This paper proposes heteroskedasticity-robust versions of the LIML and Fuller (FULL) instrumental variable estimators for models with many instruments, called HLIM and HFUL, along with heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors. The estimators work by deleting own-observation (i=j) terms from the numerator of the LIML variance ratio, a jackknife approach that also yields a robust continuous updating estimator. The authors show that LIML and FULL are inconsistent under many instruments with heteroskedasticity, derive asymptotic theory under many-instrument and many-weak-instrument sequences, and report Monte Carlo results where HLIM and HFUL match LIML/FULL under homoskedasticity and have lower bias and dispersion under heteroskedasticity.
one_line: Proposes jackknifed, heteroskedasticity-robust LIML (HLIM) and Fuller (HFUL) IV estimators with robust standard errors for models with many instruments.
key_facts: LIML and FULL are inconsistent with many instruments and heteroskedasticity, while HLIM and HFUL are heteroskedasticity-robust versions.
HLIM is obtained by dropping the i = j terms from the numerator of the LIML objective function.
HLIM is invariant to normalization and can be interpreted as a linear combination of forward and reverse jackknife IV estimators.
HLIM and HFUL are as efficient as FULL and LIML under homoskedasticity and the many weak instruments sequence of Chao and Swanson (2005).
Under the many instruments sequence of Kunitomo (1980) and Bekker (1994), HLIM may be more or less efficient than LIML.
2SLS is not consistent with many instruments even under homoskedasticity, because P_ii does not go to zero, as pointed out by Bekker (1994).
LIML is consistent under heteroskedasticity when P_ii is constant, as in dummy instruments with equal group sizes (Bekker and van der Ploeg, 2005).
LIML inconsistency under heteroskedasticity arises from nonzero covariance between P_ii and gamma_i, the projection coefficients of X_i on epsilon_i.
The paper proposes a robust continuous updating estimator (RCUE) obtained by jackknifing the CUE quadratic form, with HLIM providing starting values.
Monte Carlo results: the proposed estimators perform as well as LIML or FULL under homoskedasticity and have much lower bias and dispersion under heteroskedasticity in nearly all cases considered.
HFUL has less bias and dispersion than FULL in most cases considered under heteroskedasticity.
Assumption 1 requires P_ii <= C < 1 and K tending to infinity, which implies K/n <= C.
The JIV estimator is inefficient relative to LIML and HLIM under many weak instruments, with asymptotic variance larger than HLIM's.
The research was supported by NSF Grant No. 0136869.
